seoTitle: FDD Item 1: Franchisor, Parents and Related Companies

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: Imagine your established European brand will expand through a new U.S. subsidiary. Customers may see one logo, but the subsidiary, parent company and software supplier can each have different responsibilities. A prospective partner needs to know which organisation it is dealing with. If you are the brand owner preparing the offer, you need the same clarity before you describe your support.
The FDD is a pre-sale information document. Its job here is to identify the relevant businesses and explain the business being offered, not to replace the agreements that allocate responsibility.

sections.heading: What Item 1 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 1 identifies the franchisor and specified parents, predecessors and affiliates. It also explains the business background, offered business, market and relevant industry-law context. A predecessor is an earlier business whose history falls within the item’s requirements; a group reorganisation should not be allowed to erase the history that must be described.

Read the names alongside the corporate organisation chart and the proposed contracts. Ask who grants the brand rights, who invoices the fees, who supplies software and who provides training. The fact that a parent owns a subsidiary does not, by itself, show that the parent has promised to perform the subsidiary’s obligations.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A Swedish facilities group creates a U.S. company to sell franchises. A separate group company owns its software. The sales presentation says “our group will support you,” but the proposed agreement names only the new U.S. seller.

The expansion manager draws three boxes: parent, franchise seller and software owner. Beside each box, the manager lists the rights it controls, payments it receives and work it promises to do. The team then compares that picture with Item 1 and the agreements. If software access or support depends on another company, the documents need to explain the relevant arrangement; the logo cannot answer that question.
This does not prove the offer is unsuitable. It identifies the exact responsibility that must be understood before anyone relies on the group’s reputation.

sections.heading: Map the promise to the company, not the logo
paragraphs: Continue the fictional Swedish group example. The group name is visible to customers, but three different companies appear in the operating plan. The following is a completed preparation example, not a prescribed disclosure form.
Self-check: does a shared logo make all three companies responsible for every promise? No. Match each promise to the actual company and document before relying on it.

bullets: Record each relevant company’s exact legal name, location and role.

seoTitle: FDD Item 2: Business Experience and Franchise Support

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: An owner may have built an excellent business through personal expertise and close supervision. U.S. partners, however, may need help across time zones when that owner is unavailable. Before expanding, separate “we know how to do the work” from “we have people who can teach and support someone else doing the work.”

If your company offers franchises, it is the franchisor. The independent operator is the franchisee. Item 2 helps the prospective operator understand the experience of the people behind the franchisor, while giving your management team a useful check on its own readiness.

sections.heading: What Item 2 means in practice
paragraphs: The item covers relevant directors, principal officers and people with management responsibility for franchise sales or operations. It gives their principal positions and employers over the last five years. The exact disclosure categories matter; a short biography of the founder is not a substitute for the required information about other covered people.

A job title describes a past role, not guaranteed ability or available time. Read the history against the services your business promises. Someone may be an excellent branch manager without having trained independent owners, handled franchisee disputes or supported several regions at once. Those are management questions to investigate, not extra legal qualifications created by this article.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A training business appoints its strongest branch director to lead U.S. franchise support. The director has run a company-owned branch successfully, but has never supported an independently owned business.

The owner first checks the director’s actual five-year work history for Item 2. Separately, the operations team lists the support work: onboarding, training, urgent questions, customer escalation and performance review. It estimates the hours and identifies a backup for absences.
The result might justify another hire, a slower rollout or a more limited support promise. It does not justify rewriting the biography to suggest experience the director does not have.

sections.heading: Compare a biography with capacity to deliver
paragraphs: Use the fictional branch director above. Required business history and the optional staffing assessment are related, but they answer different questions.
Self-check: may the team describe hoped-for franchise experience as past experience? No. Keep the biography factual and address a capacity gap through the delivery plan.

seoTitle: FDD Item 3: Litigation, Allegations and Case Outcomes

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A prospective partner wants to know whether relevant disputes reveal a business or relationship risk. Your team, if preparing an FDD, needs to identify which proceedings must be disclosed and explain them accurately. Both tasks require more than searching a brand name and counting results.

The same business can have a pending claim, a settlement and an older judgment. These records mean different things. A settlement can end a dispute without a contested trial; an amount ordered by a court is not proof that the money was recovered.

sections.heading: What Item 3 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 3 specifies the entities and people whose proceedings matter, the categories of claims and the relevant time periods. It includes specified pending matters, certain franchise-relationship actions and qualifying historical outcomes or orders. Those categories must be checked against the actual records rather than replaced with “list all lawsuits.”

Read a disclosure by recording the parties, court, dates, issue and procedural outcome. Keep allegations separate from findings. Check whether the record relates to the entity offering the franchise or someone else with a similar name. Other federal, state, local or foreign searches may be needed; an FDD is not a universal disputes database.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A brand’s Item 3 describes a former operator’s claim that promised support was not delivered. A sales manager dismisses it as “just a complaint,” while a prospective partner treats the claim as proof of fraud.

Both responses skip the evidence. The team obtains the identified record and checks whether the dispute is pending, settled or decided. It then asks which support promise was in issue and whether the current operating documents and staffing address that promise.

The exercise produces a focused question about support and an accurate description of the case. It does not turn an unresolved allegation into a finding or treat a blank search as proof of no disputes.

sections.heading: Read the procedural status before drawing a lesson
paragraphs: The fictional support dispute above can be investigated without treating either side’s account as a court finding. Use this comparison when reading the documented case guides linked below.
Self-check: does a settlement automatically prove the claim, or automatically mean no liability was admitted? Neither. Read the actual record and its specific terms.

seoTitle: FDD Item 4: Bankruptcy History and the FDD Date

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: An overseas group may have changed structure after financial difficulty, or a covered person may have been associated with a business that failed. A prospective U.S. operator needs the required history explained accurately, rather than hidden behind a new company name.

If you are preparing the FDD, the question is which entities, people and proceedings fall within Item 4. If you are assessing the offer, the further question is what the disclosed history means for the organisation and support commitments you see today.

sections.heading: What Item 4 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 4 addresses specified bankruptcy histories within the ten-year period before the FDD date. Its coverage includes defined entities and individuals, relevant roles and covered foreign insolvency proceedings. Do not assume that only a U.S. case or only the current franchise seller can matter.

Check the exact identity, dates, role and outcome of each relevant entry. A person’s involvement must be understood in the way the item requires; a shared surname or a general internet result is insufficient. Then read the present financial statements and commitments separately. An old proceeding does not by itself decide whether the current seller can fund its promises.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A European group establishes a new U.S. franchise seller. The team discovers an older foreign insolvency proceeding involving a business connected to a covered person.

The company secretary checks the actual proceeding, dates and the person’s role against Item 4. The finance lead separately looks at today’s seller, its assets, obligations and support budget. These two checks answer different questions: what history must be disclosed, and what resources exist now.
The team cannot omit a required historical disclosure merely because the U.S. company is new. It also should not tell readers that a historical entry proves the present company will fail.

sections.heading: Put the history and present capacity on separate lines
paragraphs: For the fictional new U.S. seller, use the dated FDD as the reference point for the stated historical period. The record below is an internal investigation aid.
Self-check: does forming a new U.S. company erase required covered history? No. Nor does a historical entry by itself prove the new company will fail.

seoTitle: FDD Item 5: Initial Fees, Payees and Refund Terms

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A brand owner may advertise one entry fee while also requiring pre-opening training, software or equipment payments. A prospective operator needs to understand the covered payments and commitments before it plans its cash. If you prepare the offer, your finance and sales teams need to describe the same arrangements.

For an overseas business, payment routes can add confusion. Money may go to the U.S. seller, a home-country parent or another related company. Start with what is actually payable and to whom, rather than treating every invoice with the same logo as one fee.

sections.heading: What Item 5 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 5 covers the specified fees, payments and commitments for goods or services received from the franchisor or an affiliate before opening, including refund conditions. Where fees are not uniform, the required range or formula and the factors determining them matter.

Read the payment conditions alongside the proposed agreements. Ask when a commitment becomes binding and what happens if the location is not approved, training is not completed or the launch stops. These are facts to obtain from the actual documents, not refund rights this guide invents. Item 7 separately addresses the broader estimated initial investment, including relevant costs beyond the amounts covered here.

Before collecting an early payment, check the independent disclosure timetable. Calling it a reservation fee, or describing it as separate from the main franchise fee, does not itself decide whether an agreement or payment triggers a disclosure requirement. Record the real purpose, recipient and timing before money changes hands.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A cleaning brand quotes an initial fee to a U.S. partner. The draft package also contains a software setup payment to a related company and pre-opening training charges.

The finance lead records each amount, payee, due event and stated refund rule. The partner then asks what cash could be lost if the opening does not proceed. This produces a more useful discussion than asking only “what is the franchise fee?”

The list is then reconciled with the broader opening budget. Rent, third-party fit-out and other initial costs do not disappear because they are not the headline fee; they belong in the relevant investment and contract review.

sections.heading: Fill one pre-opening payment record
paragraphs: Continue the fictional cleaning offer. These illustrative entries contain no invented price or refund entitlement; the actual documents supply those facts.
Self-check: is the initial fee the whole opening investment? No. Reconcile these covered payments with Item 7, and check disclosure timing before an early payment.

seoTitle: FDD Item 6: Other Fees, Royalties and Payment Triggers

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: When a business expands through independent partners, recurring fees may fund brand rights and support. The partner must still pay wages, premises costs and other operating expenses. Looking at the royalty percentage alone can therefore give both sides an incomplete picture.

As the franchisor preparing an FDD, collect the real fee arrangements from sales, finance, training and technology teams. A charge that sits in a software agreement or appears only after a later event can still be important to the required disclosure.

sections.heading: What Item 6 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 6 uses a table for fees paid to the franchisor or affiliates, or imposed or collected for third parties. It addresses the amount or formula, due date and explanatory conditions. Royalties, transfers, renewals, audits, training and technology may require attention depending on the actual offer.

Translate each line into a cash question. Is it a regular cost, a one-off event cost or a cost that depends on conduct? What number is the formula applied to? When must it be paid? The actual documents determine the answer; this article does not assume every brand charges each example fee. Keep fees distinct from taxes and other independent legal obligations.

Where a fee may increase, the rule calls for the formula determining the increase or its maximum amount. A percentage-of-gross-sales fee needs a definition of gross sales. That contractual definition may differ from cash collected or an accounting revenue figure, particularly where refunds, taxes, bad debts or national accounts are involved. Check who can change the fee instead of assuming today’s price is fixed.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A facilities operator models only its regular royalty and concludes that a U.S. unit can fund a manager. During document review, the team also identifies technology charges and event-based training costs.

For illustration only, suppose the actual agreement charges a 6% royalty on a defined sales amount of $10,000 for a month. The royalty calculation is $10,000 × 0.06 = $600. Finance still needs the contract’s definition of sales and the payment date; this arithmetic does not tell it when customers will pay. Technology charges and event-based training costs are considered separately rather than disappearing into that royalty figure.

A fee table does not prove the unit is profitable. The useful result is a more complete model that shows the fees, other operating costs and any amounts that remain unknown instead of treating them as zero.

sections.heading: Separate recurring charges from event costs
paragraphs: Use the fictional fee model above. The royalty arithmetic is already known on its stated assumptions; other charges still need their own amount, formula and due event.
Self-check: does a correct $600 royalty calculation prove the unit is profitable? No. It answers one fee line, not the other costs or collection timing.

seoTitle: FDD Item 7: Estimated Initial Investment and Opening Cash

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A headline entry fee does not pay every opening bill. A U.S. unit may also need premises, equipment, training, insurance and cash for the period before collections cover its expenses. A brand owner preparing an FDD must assemble the prescribed estimate; a prospective operator must decide whether its own plan is adequately funded.

These are related but different exercises. The disclosure uses stated estimates and assumptions. Your business plan uses the actual site, employment plan, suppliers and payment timing as those facts become known.

sections.heading: What Item 7 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 7 uses an estimated-investment table showing relevant categories, payment methods, timing and recipients. Its additional-funds category addresses other required expenses before operations and during a stated initial operating period, with the basis for the estimate explained. The rule describes a reasonable initial period as at least three months or a reasonable period for the industry; do not mistake opening day for the end of cash needs.

Read the estimate’s assumptions before comparing its total with available funds. A site may need different work, opening can take longer and customers may pay after services are delivered. Those facts require a dated cash plan. They do not automatically mean that the published estimate is wrong, but an untested estimate is not proof that your particular plan is funded.

Check what the additional-funds allowance already includes before you use it in a cash model. If a manager cost or operating reserve is already included, adding the same amount again would double-count it. Equally, do not assume the allowance covers a cost that its stated basis leaves out.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A service unit expects to spend $80,000 establishing the business. Its owners have $100,000 and initially assume the remaining $20,000 is enough for operations.

They then estimate an illustrative $10,000 monthly cash gap while sales and collections build. In that scenario, $20,000 covers only two such months. A delayed opening or slower collection would change the result. These figures teach the calculation; they are not typical costs or a forecast for this industry.
The team compares its assumptions with Item 7, dates the actual payments and records missing quotes. It does not fill an unknown insurance or manager cost with zero simply to make the total fit.

seoTitle: FDD Item 8: Purchasing Restrictions and Approved Suppliers

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A brand may want every unit to use consistent equipment, ingredients or software. That can protect the customer experience, but it can also create costs and dependencies for an overseas expansion. A product available in your home market may be expensive to deliver in the United States or require a separate regulatory check.
The FDD’s role is to disclose the required arrangements. Your operating team’s job is to work out whether those arrangements can be supplied reliably and affordably for the proposed U.S. business.

sections.heading: What Item 8 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 8 addresses required purchases or leases, approved suppliers, specifications, approval procedures and relevant revenues or benefits received by the brand or related companies. Read both the written restrictions and the arrangements actually used in practice. A purchase requirement should not disappear from the analysis because it is communicated during training rather than in the main agreement.

Distinguish permission to buy from a supplier from permission to sell or use a regulated product. Brand approval is a private system decision. Import, safety, labelling or professional-use requirements may come from other authorities and need their own check. The exact requirements depend on the actual product and activity.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A European maintenance brand requires a particular cleaning chemical. Its U.S. partner proposes a locally available substitute that appears cheaper.

The operations manager checks the stated supplier-approval process and the performance specification. Finance compares the delivered cost, rather than comparing only the supplier’s unit price. The relevant technical person separately checks applicable product and use requirements.

Until those questions are answered, “local substitute” is only a proposal. Equally, the brand should not describe its home-market supplier as the only lawful source merely because it prefers that supplier.

sections.heading: Two approvals can answer different questions
paragraphs: In the fictional chemical-substitute example, a locally available product is only a proposal until the relevant questions are answered.
Self-check: is the preferred home-market supplier therefore the only lawful source? No. A private preference and a legal product requirement are separate questions.

seoTitle: FDD Item 9: Franchisee Obligations and Contract References

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A business can be described as manager-run while still having many obligations that someone must perform: training, staffing, insurance, reporting and payments. A founder may expect the local partner or manager to handle them, while the contract assigns responsibility differently.

Item 9 gives a structured starting point for finding those obligations. For a brand owner preparing the offer, it is also a way to check that the disclosure and agreements point to the same operating responsibilities.

sections.heading: What Item 9 means in practice
paragraphs: The item cross-references principal franchisee obligations to the agreements and relevant FDD items. Treat each reference as a direction to read the actual provision. A table label such as “training” does not tell you who must attend, when, at whose cost or what happens if a manager changes.

Separate a contractual responsibility from an internal job assignment. Your team can ask a manager to do the work, but that does not automatically change which party remains responsible under the agreement. Likewise, a contractual allocation does not answer every independent employment, tax or licensing duty.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. An owner plans to remain in Singapore while a U.S. manager runs a service unit. The owner reads Item 9 and assumes every listed task can simply be delegated.

The team follows the training reference to the actual agreement and then reads Item 15’s participation information. It checks which person must be trained, who approves a replacement and which reporting duties remain with the operating business. The precise answers come from the actual documents.

The resulting responsibility chart names the person doing each task, the party that remains responsible and the backup if the person leaves. That is more useful than marking “manager handles compliance” beside every line.

sections.heading: Follow one reference all the way to responsibility
paragraphs: Continue the fictional remote-owner training example. This completed row is a navigation exercise, not a substitute for the actual agreement.
Self-check: does writing “manager handles compliance” change the contractual party’s obligations? No. Separate the person doing the work from the party responsible for it.

seoTitle: FDD Item 10: Franchisor Financing and Repayment Terms

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: An overseas brand may help a partner pay an initial fee or obtain equipment. A lower opening payment can make a plan appear easier to fund, but the amount deferred still needs to be paid on the stated terms. Later repayments compete with wages, rent and other business cash needs.

If you prepare the franchise offer, collect the actual financing arrangements rather than describing them only as a sales benefit. If you assess an offer, read the loan or credit documents alongside the franchise agreement.

sections.heading: What Item 10 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 10 addresses covered direct or indirect financing by the franchisor, agents or affiliates. Relevant terms include interest, charges, repayment, security, guarantees, default consequences and relevant assignment or lender benefits. “Default” means a failure to meet an obligation as defined in the actual documents; do not assume that every agreement uses the same conditions.

Ask what happens throughout the life of the arrangement, not just at opening. How are payments calculated? Who must pay? What supports the debt? Can the financing be assigned to another creditor? The disclosure identifies required information, while the actual agreement determines the specific transaction terms.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A brand allows a U.S. partner to defer part of an opening payment. The partner treats the deferral as a reduction in the total opening cost.

Finance shows the distinction with two columns: cash paid now and cash owed later. It then adds the actual repayment schedule and charges to the cash plan. No illustrative interest rate is assumed to apply to the real offer.

The company secretary reads any guarantee and security documents. The team asks whether a delay in opening would change the ability to make repayments, rather than assuming that the brand’s involvement removes normal debt risk.

sections.heading: Compare less cash now with obligations later
paragraphs: The fictional deferred opening payment is not automatically a discount. Complete the comparison using the actual financing documents, without assuming an interest rate.
Self-check: would a delayed opening necessarily delay the debt payments? Do not assume so. Read the actual terms and test the payment dates against the cash plan.

seoTitle: FDD Item 11: Assistance, Advertising, Systems and Training

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A partner may hear “we provide training and ongoing support” and imagine daily help. Your team may mean a short initial course and occasional remote contact. That difference matters before a U.S. agreement is sold, especially when the support team is in another time zone.

As the franchisor, use Item 11 to explain the support arrangements the rule requires. Separately, build an internal delivery plan so the people, budget and coverage behind your promises actually exist.

sections.heading: What Item 11 means in practice
paragraphs: The item describes specified pre-opening and continuing assistance, advertising, computer systems and training, with relevant agreement references. Read what is promised, what has conditions and what is optional. A general sales statement should not replace the actual disclosure and contract detail.

For each important service, ask who provides it, to whom, when and by what method. Training a manager, maintaining software and visiting a site can require different people and costs. Do not infer a particular service frequency or guaranteed result where the actual documents do not provide it.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A European facilities brand promises U.S. field support. Its current support manager already covers the home network and normally works during European business hours.

The operations lead lists the actual pre-opening and continuing tasks described in the offer. It then identifies who can answer urgent U.S. questions, who can travel, how absences are covered and how the work is funded. A remote helpdesk and an on-site visit are not treated as interchangeable services.

If the plan cannot support the stated promise, the team must address the delivery gap before relying on optimistic sales language. This is a management decision informed by the disclosure, not proof that every foreign brand needs the same staffing model.

sections.heading: Turn a support promise into a delivery row
paragraphs: Use the fictional overseas field-support promise. These are optional management rows for testing delivery capacity, not extra legal service frequencies.
Self-check: can remote helpdesk availability simply be counted as a promised site visit? No. Match the actual service to the people and resources that can deliver it.

seoTitle: FDD Item 12: Franchise Territory and Exclusivity

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A map can look simple while the business is not. A local operator may serve customers inside a boundary, the brand may retain national customers and another channel may take online orders. Without clear definitions, two parties can each believe that the same sale belongs to them.

For an overseas brand expanding through partners, territory design is therefore both a disclosure issue and an operating decision. The FDD describes the relevant rights and limits; the contracts and actual customer arrangements need to fit that explanation.

sections.heading: What Item 12 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 12 covers location and territory, exclusivity and conditions, relocation or additional rights, reserved channels and relevant competing operations. Read the actual language rather than assuming that the word “exclusive” protects every activity within a coloured area.

Ask what protection is offered, what the franchisor retains and what conditions keep the right in place. Then distinguish competition from the brand’s own system from competition by unrelated businesses. A franchise territory is not a government grant preventing all independent competitors from trading nearby.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A Dutch business-services brand gives a U.S. partner a stated local territory while retaining a national customer whose sites fall inside it.

The team maps the customer sites, sales channel, service responsibility and payment arrangements. It checks the actual territory and national-account provisions to see who may sell, who must deliver the work and who receives the revenue. The map alone cannot decide those questions.

The parties then compare the explanation in Item 12 with the proposed agreement and operating instructions. Any unresolved allocation remains a question to settle, rather than a verbal assurance that “the territory is protected.”

sections.heading: Map a national account inside the local boundary
paragraphs: Continue the fictional Dutch business-services example. The map boundary alone does not allocate a national customer’s sale, work and payment.
Self-check: does an exclusive franchise territory stop every unrelated competitor from trading there? No. Read the precise private rights and their conditions.

seoTitle: FDD Item 13: Trademarks, Ownership and U.S. Rights

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: Your brand may be well established in Europe or Southeast Asia while being new to the United States. A prospective U.S. partner will rely on using that identity. It therefore matters who controls the rights, what the recorded status is and what happens if the name becomes disputed.

If your group uses a separate company to own the brand, identify that company and the arrangement allowing the franchise seller and operators to use the relevant marks. The sales company and the intellectual-property owner should not be treated as interchangeable merely because they are related.

sections.heading: What Item 13 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 13 identifies principal trademarks, registration or application status and relevant disputes, limits and protection obligations. Read the actual disclosures about the marks offered, not simply a certificate or logo from the home market.

Registration and freedom to use answer related but different questions. A registration record does not replace the inquiry into the proposed U.S. use and relevant competing rights. Also read what the documents say about protecting the mark or changing its use. This item describes required information; it does not guarantee that no dispute will arise.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A European service brand has used its name for years and wants its new U.S. subsidiary to sell franchises under that name. Management assumes the home-country registration is enough.

The company secretary identifies the actual owner of the mark, the U.S. registration or application position and the relevant disclosures. The team separately obtains the needed U.S. clearance assessment and checks the agreement allowing the subsidiary and operators to use the brand.
The result is a clear record of the rights and unresolved questions. It is not a promise that an application will succeed or that a familiar name can never face a challenge.

sections.heading: Separate the evidence about brand rights
paragraphs: Apply the fictional European-brand example. The record below helps the team explain what is known; it does not itself supply a clearance opinion.

seoTitle: FDD Item 14: Patents, Copyright and Proprietary Information

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: An overseas business may describe its operating system as “our know-how.” In practice, the system can combine internally written methods, a consultant’s training material, licensed software and other content. U.S. operators need the relevant rights and arrangements to use what the brand supplies.
For the brand owner preparing an offer, Item 14 is a reason to identify the actual materials and rights rather than treating a finished manual as proof that the group owns everything inside it.

sections.heading: What Item 14 means in practice
paragraphs: The item addresses material patent and copyright rights and applications, relevant limits or proceedings, and protection obligations. It also describes the general nature of confidential proprietary information. Read the complete prescribed item for the required categories and detail.

Separate ownership from permission to use. Your company may have created material itself, acquired rights or received a limited licence from another supplier. The terms may differ by user, country, activity or duration. An FDD explanation is not a substitute for reading those arrangements, and it does not settle independent customer-data or privacy obligations.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A training brand has a manual produced by its own staff, videos commissioned from a consultant and an online platform supplied by a software company. It plans to give U.S. partners access to the whole package.

The operations manager lists each component. The company secretary then checks who owns it, what permission the brand has and whether the proposed operator use fits that permission. Finance identifies the recurring costs of supplying the package.

This review may reveal a permission to obtain or a supplier term to clarify. It avoids the unsupported statement that ownership of one manual gives the brand all the rights required for every part of the system.

sections.heading: Inventory the components, not just the finished manual
paragraphs: Use the fictional training package. Knowing that one component belongs to the brand does not establish the permissions for every other component.
Self-check: does ownership of the manual establish ownership of the platform? No. Also keep customer-data duties separate from intellectual-property permission.

seoTitle: FDD Item 15: Owner Participation and Manager-Run Franchises

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: An established brand owner may be used to employing branch managers. A franchise arrangement can allocate responsibilities differently. The operator may have to participate personally, or the proposed manager may have to meet particular conditions. Those questions need answering before anyone assumes the owner can remain remote.
As the franchisor preparing the offer, explain the required or recommended involvement accurately. As a prospective operator, compare it with the people who will actually run the business.

sections.heading: What Item 15 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 15 addresses personal participation obligations or recommendations, including obligations arising from written agreements or the franchisor’s practice. Reading the contract alone may therefore miss a requirement imposed through how the system actually operates.

Where personal on-premises supervision is not required, the item asks for specific information. For an individual franchisee, disclose whether the brand recommends on-premises supervision by that person. Explain limits on whom the operator can hire as supervisor and whether the supervisor must complete the brand’s training. For a business-entity franchisee, explain any equity interest the supervisor must hold. Do not turn these conditional disclosure questions into a statement that every franchise has the same manager conditions.

Separately, Item 15 requires disclosure of restrictions that the franchisee must place on its manager, such as confidentiality or a stated noncompetition requirement. That disclosure duty is not confined to the situation where personal on-premises supervision is unnecessary. Describing a restriction does not decide whether it can be enforced under other applicable law.

A permitted manager is not free capacity. Include the real cost of salary, employer costs, benefits, cover and relevant training in the business model. Separately check any immigration or employment question raised by the actual work and people.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. An owner in Singapore plans to keep running the home business while a U.S. manager handles the new unit. The owner assumes any experienced employee can replace that manager during absence.

The team reads Item 15 and the relevant agreements. It records whether personal participation is required or recommended, the manager’s required training, any ownership condition and the replacement process. It then asks who covers illness or resignation and how that person qualifies.

Finance includes the complete manager cost rather than using profit from a unit where the owner does the work without a wage. The resulting plan may support remote ownership, or show a gap to solve; the marketing label alone cannot decide.

sections.heading: Keep the supervision branch and manager restrictions separate
paragraphs: For the fictional Singapore owner, begin with the actual participation obligations or recommendations, including system practice. The conditional disclosure questions below are not uniform conditions imposed on every franchise.

Self-check: does disclosure of a noncompetition restriction establish that it is enforceable? No. Disclosure and enforceability are separate questions, just as permission to hire a manager is separate from funding one.

seoTitle: FDD Item 16: Products, Services and Customer Restrictions

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A service business often wins work by combining related tasks. Your home-market offer may include cleaning, maintenance and technical work in one package. The U.S. franchise documents may authorise a different range, and particular tasks may raise separate operating-permission questions.
This matters to both sides. The brand owner needs a clear and deliverable offer, while the independent operator needs to know what it may sell before estimating demand and revenue.

sections.heading: What Item 16 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 16 describes relevant restrictions on goods or services, customer access, required offerings and the franchisor’s rights to change the authorised range. Read the actual conditions instead of assuming that an attractive service category includes every related task.

Separate a private system restriction from a public legal restriction. The brand can describe what it allows under its arrangement; the relevant authority determines applicable government permissions. A product or technical service can therefore need both the correct contractual right and its separate activity-specific review.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A facilities partner sees demand for mechanical maintenance and wants to add it to an existing cleaning offer. The partner assumes that the brand’s general service label covers the proposed work.

The operations lead first lists the actual tasks and checks the authorised range and customer conditions. The technical lead then identifies the separate qualification or permission questions for those tasks and locations. Neither check is treated as a substitute for the other.
The team updates the commercial model only when it knows which services it can actually offer through the proposed arrangement. It does not count uncertain technical work as guaranteed revenue.

sections.heading: Test the added service on two separate tracks
paragraphs: Use the fictional cleaning operator’s proposed mechanical maintenance. Do not put revenue from an unresolved service into the model as a confirmed result.

seoTitle: FDD Item 17: Renewal, Termination, Transfer and Disputes

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: Expansion discussions naturally focus on opening. A long relationship also needs a plan for later changes: a partner may want to sell, the brand may change its model, an agreement may expire or a dispute may arise. These events can affect the value and continuity of the business.
If your company offers franchises, prepare a consistent explanation of the relevant terms. If you assess an offer, follow the summary to the actual agreements before relying on a short description.

sections.heading: What Item 17 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 17 summarises specified provisions with contract references, including term, renewal, termination, transfer, noncompetition and dispute arrangements. Treat it as a map of the documents. The actual clause contains the relevant conditions, steps and consequences.

Then check independent state protections. Disclosure of a clause does not establish its enforceability or remove a protection that the applicable law does not allow the parties to waive. This article does not supply one universal notice, cure or exit rule for every U.S. state and relationship.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A European brand expects a successful U.S. partner to renew automatically. The partner expects to sell the business freely after a few years. Both rely on their commercial conversation rather than the documents.

The team reads the Item 17 renewal and transfer summaries, then the referenced clauses. It records each relevant consent, deadline, payment and other condition. It also checks the state-law questions for the actual relationship and location.
The result may show that a future event requires advance preparation. It does not justify telling either party that a summary guarantees renewal or that every written restriction is enforceable.

sections.heading: Separate future events before reading their conditions
paragraphs: For the fictional brand and partner, these are different document enquiries. This is not a universal state-law timetable.
Self-check: does reaching the scheduled expiry date mean the same thing as early termination? No. Identify the intended event before choosing documents, dates and further state research.

seoTitle: FDD Item 18: Public Figures, Benefits and Management Roles

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A recognisable person can make an unfamiliar overseas brand seem more established in a new market. A prospective operator may assume that public visibility means the offer has been checked or that the person is involved in its day-to-day delivery.

The useful first step is to identify what the person actually does and what relationship the documents describe. If your company prepares the offer, accurate disclosure should replace vague claims about who is “behind the brand.”

sections.heading: What Item 18 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 18 addresses compensation or benefits given or promised for use of a public figure in the franchise name or symbol, or for endorsing or recommending the franchise to prospective operators. It also addresses relevant management involvement and investment, including the stated value of services. The actual role and purpose matter: an ordinary consumer product advertisement should not automatically be treated as the same arrangement as promoting a franchise offer.

Read the stated role separately from the business evidence. A person may promote the brand without managing the support team. An investment may show one financial connection without proving the proposed unit’s results. Item 19 and the financial disclosures answer their own questions; an endorsement does not replace them.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A service network features a well-known presenter in its recruitment material. A prospective U.S. partner assumes the presenter supervises training and has reviewed the unit economics.

The team reads the relevant disclosures and identifies the person’s actual role, benefits and investment information. It then separately asks who delivers training and what evidence supports financial claims. It does not infer operational responsibility from a photograph or slogan.
This allows the brand’s promotional arrangement to be understood for what it is. It avoids turning public recognition into an unsupported guarantee of business performance or legal compliance.

sections.heading: Compare public visibility with the actual role
paragraphs: In the fictional presenter example, use the disclosure to identify the relationship rather than filling gaps from a photograph.
Self-check: does appearing in recruitment material show that the person supervises training? No. Follow the actual role and the independent support disclosures.

seoTitle: FDD Item 19: Financial Performance Representations and Earnings

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A home-market business may have strong sales and an owner who does much of the work personally. Those numbers can look attractive in a U.S. recruitment presentation. They do not automatically describe a U.S. unit that must pay a manager, local wages and the fees in the proposed arrangement.

If you are the franchisor, making a financial claim is a disclosure and evidence decision, not simply a marketing choice. If you are assessing an offer, the first task is to understand what the disclosed figures actually measure.

sections.heading: What Item 19 means in practice
paragraphs: The brand may elect not to make a financial performance representation, but that does not mean it can omit Item 19 itself. Where a representation is made, the rule requires a reasonable basis and written substantiation at the time it is made, together with the relevant detail and qualifications.

The representation must be included in Item 19 with the required supporting disclosures. Choosing not to make a representation does not authorise a salesperson to make financial performance claims orally, in an advertisement or on a separate spreadsheet. The rule has specific treatment for actual records of an existing outlet being considered for purchase and for properly identified supplemental representations; those provisions have their own conditions and are not general permission for off-document earnings claims. Written support alone does not replace the required disclosure.

For historical figures, identify the units included and excluded, the period, unit type and relevant differences. For projections, understand the stated assumptions. Company-owned units, franchised units and founder-operated units may have different costs. An average can also hide large differences between individual units.

Use the disclosed information as evidence to examine, not as permission to invent a new sales promise. Keep actual source figures separate from your own explicitly labelled planning assumptions and read the complete item for the prescribed content and qualifications.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional arithmetic example. A hypothetical unit has annual revenue of $1,000,000 and $180,000 left before two costs that have not yet been included: a manager and a royalty. This is not a real brand result or an earnings forecast.

Suppose, purely for this exercise, the complete annual manager cost is $120,000 and the royalty is 6% of revenue. The royalty is $1,000,000 × 0.06 = $60,000. Subtracting both gives $180,000 − $120,000 − $60,000 = $0 before any other omitted costs.

The lesson is not that a particular franchise earns nothing. It is that a number described as profit or surplus can change completely when you identify the costs it excludes. Do not subtract a cost twice if it was already included; first establish the definition of the starting figure.

seoTitle: FDD Item 20: Outlets, Closures and Franchisee Information

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A growing network can sound reassuring to an overseas owner planning U.S. expansion. But a single total can conceal very different events: new units open, existing units close, ownership changes and agreements end. Those events raise different business questions.

The franchisor preparing an FDD must use the prescribed categories and information. A reader assessing the network should understand those categories before drawing a conclusion from a sales presentation.

sections.heading: What Item 20 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 20 contains outlet tables and specified current and former franchisee information, with defined categories and periods. Read the table headings, dates and type of outlet. Do not combine company-owned and franchised units or different reporting periods without understanding the difference.

A net increase can coexist with terminations, non-renewals and transfers. Those events do not all mean the same thing and do not, without further evidence, establish either success or failure. The contacts and records described in the item can help identify questions to investigate, but no single discussion or table supplies a complete picture.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional arithmetic example. A hypothetical network starts with 20 units, adds eight and has five leave the counted population during the period. On those simplified assumptions, the ending total is 23 and net growth is three.

That headline does not explain why the five left or whether the eight new units are operating as expected. The team reads the actual categories rather than calling every departure a failure. It also asks whether the support team grew in capacity as the system expanded.

The useful result is a set of evidence questions tied to the disclosed period and categories. It is not a probability of success for the proposed U.S. partner, and these illustrative numbers are not real network data.

paragraphs: These figures restate the simplified fictional example. The category “leave the counted population” is not a finding that five businesses failed.

Self-check: should every transfer be treated as an outlet closure? No. Follow the prescribed actual table categories. A change in owner and a change in the counted outlet total are different questions.

seoTitle: FDD Item 21: Financial Statements, Audits and Guarantees

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: A foreign group may have a substantial home business and a small new U.S. selling subsidiary. U.S. operators will need to understand which business is responsible for support and what financial information and commitments are disclosed.

The FDD therefore needs more than a general statement that the group is successful. If you prepare the offer, identify the correct reporting entities and obtain appropriate accounting advice. If you assess it, read the financial information for the actual parties involved.

sections.heading: What Item 21 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 21 specifies financial statements, audit standards and treatment of relevant affiliates, parents and subfranchisors. The current rule addresses U.S. generally accepted accounting principles or treatment permitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission, together with applicable audit and other requirements. A home-country audit does not automatically establish that the prescribed U.S. disclosure requirements are satisfied.

For a first reading, distinguish the main reports. A balance sheet describes a financial position at a date. An income statement describes performance over a period. A cash-flow statement helps explain cash movements. Read the entity name, dates, accountant’s report and relevant notes before comparing numbers.

Then examine any disclosed guarantee or other support commitment. Group ownership alone should not be treated as an enforceable promise by the parent. Strong past accounts also do not guarantee that the company will have every resource needed for future expansion.

sections.heading: Understand the reporting periods and the limited alternatives
paragraphs: Under the ordinary requirements, the balance sheets cover the previous two fiscal year-ends, while operations, stockholders’ equity and cash-flow statements cover the previous three fiscal years. A fiscal year is the business’s accounting year, which need not end in December. Compare the same entity and periods rather than mixing a parent’s current figures with an older subsidiary report.

The affiliate alternative has precise conditions. The affiliate statements must meet the specified requirements, and the affiliate must absolutely and unconditionally guarantee all of the franchisor’s obligations to the franchisee under the franchise agreement. The guarantee need not cover third parties, and a copy is attached to the disclosure. Ordinary group ownership or a limited support letter is not that guarantee. Separate parent or subfranchisor statement requirements can also apply.

A start-up franchise system without audited statements may use the rule’s limited phase-in. The stages below are conditional, not a general exemption from financial disclosure. The franchisor must prepare audited statements as soon as practicable, use an unaudited format conforming as closely as possible to audited statements, and provide the required unaudited history or conspicuous explanation of its shorter business history. Do not assume a newly formed U.S. seller qualifies merely because it is new.

The finance lead identifies the financial statements required for the offer, their reporting periods and accounting treatment. The company secretary then checks the actual commitments connecting the parent to the seller. The team does not assume that every parent asset is cash available to the subsidiary.

seoTitle: FDD Item 22: Contracts, Exhibits and Agreement Versions

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: An expansion team may negotiate a headline fee and territory while other obligations sit in a guarantee, software contract, lease or purchase document. Different members of the team can therefore be reviewing different versions of what they believe is one deal.

If your company prepares the FDD, assemble the proposed agreement package the item requires. If you assess the offer, make sure the people reviewing cost, operations and legal terms have the relevant documents, rather than only the main contract.

sections.heading: What Item 22 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 22 attaches proposed agreements regarding the offering, including the franchise agreement and relevant lease, option or purchase agreements. Read the complete prescribed item to establish the actual attachment requirements for the offer; this article is not a universal list of every possible document.

An attachment gives the reader material to examine. It does not mean a government agency has approved its terms. Also compare the names, dates and versions across the package. Two documents can allocate different responsibilities or use terms that only become clear when read together.

Keep a record of later changes to fees, guarantees and related terms. A changed signing package can raise separate disclosure and timing questions. Before scheduling signature or payment, compare the actual new version with what was delivered and arrange the relevant material-change and timing check; an updated exhibit index alone does not settle that question.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A service brand and a U.S. partner agree the commercial points in a short email. The main franchise agreement appears to reflect them, but the wider pack also contains software terms and a guarantee.

The expansion manager creates a document index. Finance identifies every relevant payment commitment; operations identifies service and system dependencies; the responsible legal reviewer examines the actual obligations and parties. Any differences from the commercial discussion are recorded for resolution.
The team keeps version control so a late revised attachment is not missed. This is an organised review of the actual package, not a claim that reading one document settles all other commitments.

paragraphs: Continue the fictional email/main agreement/software/guarantee example. The table is an internal document index, not a universal list of prescribed exhibits.

Self-check: does updating the exhibit index settle a later agreement-change issue? No. The index helps find the actual difference; the separate disclosure and timing question still needs its own check.

seoTitle: FDD Item 23: Receipts and Disclosure Delivery Records

sections.heading: Why this matters for your expansion
paragraphs: Disclosure duties depend on giving the right information through the relevant process. A signature on a receipt is useful evidence, but the team still needs to know what document was delivered and whether the required attachments were included.

For the franchisor preparing an offer, this is a document-control responsibility. For the recipient, signing the prescribed receipt should not be confused with signing the franchise agreement or deciding that the business is suitable.

sections.heading: What Item 23 means in practice
paragraphs: Item 23 requires two copies of the prescribed detachable acknowledgement as the last pages of the FDD. The required receipt text is prescribed, so a short homemade statement saying “information received” is not a substitute. The receipt identifies the issuance date, the exhibits and the relevant franchise sellers’ names, principal business addresses and telephone numbers. It also addresses the registered agent’s name and address if not already disclosed as specified by the rule.

The receipt lists the titles of attached exhibits and provides space for the prospective franchisee’s signature and date. The franchisor may include instructions for returning it. In practical terms, this lets the parties connect an acknowledgement with a particular disclosure package; it does not prove that the recipient completed a review of every term.

Match the receipt to the actual dated FDD and attachment package. Keep delivery facts distinct from the later decision to sign an agreement or make a payment. Applicable federal and state timing requirements need their own check; a receipt is not government approval or a substitute for that analysis.

Do not treat acknowledgement as a general waiver of the prospect’s rights. It records the relevant delivery information; it does not prove that the person has read, understood or accepted every commercial and legal risk.

sections.heading: Fictional worked example
paragraphs: Fictional example. A brand emails a document folder to a prospective U.S. operator and later obtains a signed receipt. During review, the team finds that two different dated FDD files have been circulating.

The team reconstructs the actual delivery record: recipient, date, document version and attachments. It checks the receipt against that record, then separately checks the applicable disclosure timetable. It does not change an uncertain delivery date simply to make a planned signing date work.

The purpose is an accurate record. If something is missing or inconsistent, the issue remains to be resolved through the proper process; a signature should not be used to turn uncertainty into a fictional history.

sections.heading: Reconstruct the fictional two-version delivery
paragraphs: Use the existing scenario in which two dated FDD files circulate. These are delivery-log questions; this table is not a replacement for the prescribed receipt.
Self-check: may the team replace an uncertain delivery date with the date needed for signing? No. Preserve the uncertainty and reconcile the actual records rather than inventing a history.

rows: Initial delivery
Actual recipient, date, FDD version and attachments
That a different version or missing exhibit was also furnished
Signed prescribed receipt
The actual acknowledgement and identified package
That every term was read, accepted or waived
Planned agreement or payment
The relevant event and its actual date
That the independent federal and state timetable has been satisfied

sections.heading: How your team can use this information
bullets: Identify the actual FDD date and complete exhibit package.
Use and retain the prescribed receipt and accurate delivery record.
Reconcile recipients, document versions and delivery dates.
Check agreement and payment timing separately, preserving any unresolved facts.
